methodological_rigor.justification: Well-designed cross-sectional survey with large, representative sample (N=3,348). Proper use of Best-Worst Scaling with both counting and conditional regression approaches. Confidence intervals and odds ratios appropriately reported. Data cleaning procedures documented with 358 careless responses identified and removed. Limitations section acknowledges online bias and underpowered subgroup analyses, demonstrating appropriate methodological awareness.

clinical_relevance_loe.justification: Directly addresses implementation barriers for HPV-based cervical screening policy transition in Canada. Findings explicitly intended to guide health jurisdiction decision-making and public health messaging. High relevance to clinical practice and health system implementation. Clear translational pathway from preferences to policy-informed education and communication strategies.

reporting_quality.justification: Explicitly reports STROBE compliance (Appendix A referenced). Comprehensive reporting of study design, eligibility criteria, data collection procedures, statistical methods, and results with detailed tables. Clear description of BWS methodology and analytical approach. However, data and code availability statements are absent from the manuscript, limiting reproducibility.

novelty_literature.justification: First nationally representative Canadian study assessing women's cervical screening preferences during HPV implementation transition. Extends prior pilot work (N=1,027) to larger, pan-Canadian sample with deliberate oversampling of underscreened populations. Novel application of Best-Worst Scaling to preference elicitation in this context. Meaningfully addresses identified evidence-implementation gap.

writing_presentation.justification: Well-structured manuscript with clear progression from introduction through discussion. Effective use of tables (6 main results tables) and flow diagram for participant selection. Precise technical language appropriate for methods section. Discussion effectively synthesizes findings and acknowledges limitations. Minor opportunities for brevity in methods section but overall publication-ready presentation.

key_strengths: Large, nationally representative sample with deliberate oversampling of underscreened women, addressing health equity priority population
Rigorous use of Best-Worst Scaling methodology with both counting and conditional regression approaches, providing robust preference quantification
Clear policy relevance for Canadian HPV screening implementation with identified preference-policy misalignment requiring targeted interventions
Comprehensive subgroup analyses demonstrating heterogeneity in preferences by language, age, ethnicity, income, and gender identity
Full STROBE adherence with transparent reporting of methods, limitations, and data cleaning procedures
key_concerns: Data and code availability not addressed, limiting reproducibility and open science practices
Online survey methodology may underrepresent populations without internet access or digital literacy, despite acknowledging this limitation
Stated preferences in survey context may not translate to real-world screening behavior once implementation and education occur
Underscreened population still likely healthier/more digitally literate than true hardest-to-reach populations
Limited mechanistic insight into drivers of preference differences between adequately and underscreened groups beyond demographic factors
chief_reviewer.rationale: Solid implementation science study with methodologically appropriate design, clear policy relevance, and rigorous reporting. Suitable for Tier 2 journals (JCO, ESMO Open) due to methodological rigor and direct health system applicability, though incremental contribution and limited novel mechanistic insight prevent Tier 1 consideration. Minor data availability statement addition would support publication.
